extracted.intended_audience: aspiring op-ed and letter-to-the-editor writers pitching national and local news outlets
extracted.subtask_description: Practical submission and content guidelines for writing and pitching op-eds and letters to a wide range of national and local news outlets, including outlet-specific length, format, exclusivity, contact, and verification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate publication and check recent coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: We suggest that you choose a publication and then read recent issues/posts to see if your idea/topic has been covered recently. If so, another outlet might be a better fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick the outlet that best matches your topic and audience; avoid pitching ideas already covered recently in that outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find editors and contact information via X/Twitter
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re interested in a publication not listed here, we suggest searching the name of the news outlet and the words “opinion” and “editor” on X’s (formerly known as Twitter) search bar and looking under the “people” vertical when the search results come up. Most editors list their contact information in their X/Twitter bio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social profiles to find up-to-date editor contact details when the site's guidelines are not explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available mentor/editor programs and workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase your chances of publication, join Ask A Journalist office hours or attend workshops to have drafts live-edited and to access journalist mentors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take advantage of live editing and mentorship to strengthen pitch and draft before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow outlet-specific word-count limits for op-eds
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets specify a maximum or preferred word length for op-eds (examples: 500, 550, 600, 650, 700, 750, 800, up to 1000+ words depending on outlet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere precisely to each publication’s stated limit (e.g., 'The New York Times: 400-1200 words', 'Los Angeles Times: about 750 words', 'USA Today: 650-900 words', 'Wall Street Journal: 600-1200 words', 'Seattle Times: no longer than 650 words'). When in doubt, keep it concise and within the outlet’s stated range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow outlet-specific word/character limits for letters to the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Each outlet sets short limits for letters (common values: 150–300 words; some use characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep letters within the outlet's limit (e.g., 'Letters: 150-200 words', 'Newsday: Max. 5000 characters', 'The New York Times: preferably 150–175 words').

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full contact and verification information
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets require full name, mailing address/home address (city/hometown), and daytime phone number and/or email for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include name, full home mailing address (or city), day and evening phone numbers, and email in submission; expect calls for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose credentials, affiliation, and relationship to the issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets often require or prefer you to 'include your position and related experience' or to 'fully disclose relationship with issue and expertise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a short biography, relevant credentials, job title/affiliation, or explanation of expertise in both the email and the piece where requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity and prior publication rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many publications require pieces be exclusive to them (e.g., 'must be exclusive to the Washington Post', 'Opinion pieces must be exclusive to Crain’s', 'Op-eds should not have been published elsewhere').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit work simultaneously to exclusive outlets. Some outlets (e.g., LARB) accept simultaneous submissions but ask to be informed if accepted elsewhere—follow outlet-specific policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paste text into email body or use plain-text online form when requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Several outlets instruct authors to paste the article into the body of the email or use their online form (e.g., 'Contents must be sent in body of email message -- plain text only', 'Paste in text', 'Text of submission in body of email or attached Word doc').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the outlet’s preferred submission method: if they ask for plain text in the body, do not send attachments; if they allow Word attachments, follow any attachment guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo/headshot requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets request or require a headshot/JPG photo with specific size recommendations (examples: 'high resolution photo', 'at least 200KB', '100 kilobytes-plus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a professional headshot when requested and obey file-type and minimum-size guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/regional preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets give preference to local/regional writers and topics (examples: 'Preference given to Atlanta and Georgia writers', 'Local topics and authors preferred', 'Preference goes to local, state, and Western regional issues').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch local outlets with local angles; emphasize residence or connection to the area to improve chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and topical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces should be timely, relate to current news or issues, or be 'of unusual interest to readers' or 'timely, original, and short.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your argument connected to current events or ongoing conversations; show why it matters now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sources, links, and attributions for facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets ask for sources for facts and quotations and sometimes prefer URLs (e.g., 'Pieces should include links (URLs, not headlines or footnotes) to back up quotes and factual material', 'Provide source material for fact checking', 'Facts should be annotated').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include URLs for studies and source material, and be prepared to provide verification for factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: No anonymous or pseudonymous submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets do not accept anonymous or pseudonymous submissions and require real names/signatures ('No anonymous submissions', 'No pseudonyms or anonymity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always submit with your real full name and contact details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlets reserve rights to edit for length/style/accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are often 'subject to editing' and may be 'edited for length, grammar and clarity' or become property of the outlet in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect editorial edits; provide clear source material to minimize factual edits and keep a copy of your original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response time / assume declined after stated window
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets state a timeframe for response and tell authors to assume decline if not contacted (examples: 'If you do not hear in three business days, assume the article will not be used', 'If you do not hear from them within 5 days they will not be using your submission').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stated response windows before reoffering the piece elsewhere; some outlets permit offering elsewhere after a given number of days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission format and technical restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific technical requirements include 'No attachments' or 'No attachments, please', 'Plain text only', 'Send as Microsoft Word attachments and pasted into the body of the email', and 'Do not send letter as an attachment—attachments will not be opened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the exact file and format rules per outlet to avoid automatic rejection or being ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include byline/brief author ID and contact details in email and attached file when requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets require a tagline or brief author ID on both the attachment and the email (e.g., 'Include name of author, and brief biography on both attachment AND email').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat biographical and contact info as requested in both email and document to ensure the editor sees it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive topical or column rules (what content is appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets specify appropriate topics and constraints: public policy, social issues, higher-education policy, science with a policy angle, non-promotional persuasive argument, not endorsements, not libelous or incendiary (e.g., Tulsa World list), and not in direct response to other op/eds for op-ed space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content to the publication’s stated topical focus and avoid prohibited content (product endorsements, election endorsements in some outlets, or direct responses where letters are appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative voice / expertise required
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets prefer pieces 'by someone in position of expertise' or 'views of an expert in a particular field' and indicate that authority or unique perspective improves consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress your expertise, experience, or relevant first-hand perspective in your bio and the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal narrative allowed or preferred in some formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain columns request personal narrative or a theme that can be summarized in a single sentence (e.g., Buffalo News 'My View' asks for personal narrative; Chronicle of Higher Education encourages personal experience-based essays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the outlet asks for personal narrative, include relevant storytelling elements and a clear thematic sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide city/hometown and occupancy info for publication and byline purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets ask that you 'include background and where you live', 'city of residence', 'hometown', or 'community of residence' as part of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include city and community details to connect your voice to the readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters should respond to recent articles when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets require letters to refer to a recent article and be submitted within a time window (e.g., NYT: 'should refer to an article that has appeared within the last seven days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to a specific story, reference it clearly and respect the outlet’s timeliness rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some outlets do not accept unsolicited op-eds
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets such as Christian Science Monitor state they are 'not accepting general, unsolicited op-eds' but accept topic-specific submissions for specific blogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether an outlet accepts unsolicited op-eds or only commissioned or topic-specific submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and submission subject-line conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional special subject-line instructions exist (example: '“My Turn” should be the subject line title' for Arizona Republic; include the topic in the subject line for LA Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the outlet’s recommended subject-line format to make editorial triage easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity and simultaneous-submission exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most outlets want exclusivity, but some accept simultaneous submissions or have explicit nuanced policies (e.g., LARB accepts simultaneous submissions but asks to be informed if accepted elsewhere; Cleveland Plain Dealer says pieces become property of cleveland.com).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the outlet’s exclusivity policy; if simultaneous submissions are allowed, clearly state that in your pitch if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ownership and copyright notes vary by outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets state authors retain rights, others state pieces become property of the site or that the outlet reserves publication rights (examples: 'Writers retain rights to their work' vs 'Pieces become property of The Bee / cleveland.com').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If retaining copyright or future reuse matters, confirm the outlet’s policy before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include links for quotes and factual material (URLs preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets request links (URLs, not headlines or footnotes) to back up quotes and factual material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide direct URLs for sources cited in the piece so editors can easily fact-check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promotional or product-endorsement content
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets prohibit product endorsement and promotional pieces (explicitly mentioned in some guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write argument-driven op-eds with public-interest emphasis, not advertorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect outlet-specific scheduling and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets require submissions by specific deadlines for certain publication days (example: Salt Lake City Tribune: 'Must arrive latest by Wednesday for publication on Saturday afternoon').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit within the outlet’s production window to be considered for the intended publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide verifiable identification for letters (signed, with address and phone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters commonly require signature and verification details: 'Must include signature, home address, and telephone number' or 'Include full name, home address and daytime and evening telephone numbers for verification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always sign letters and include contact details for verification; expect edits for length and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow outlet-specific stylistic or topical preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets have nuanced preferences (e.g., 'Conversational articles are most appealing', 'Should be well written, weighty, and whimsical', 'Focus on public policy', 'Science pieces should explore intersection with politics, economics, culture').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt tone and emphasis to each outlet’s stated voice and audience; read recent pieces to match style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-audience or section-specific guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain outlets have special submission channels and criteria (e.g., Education Week has different lengths for teachers' first-person submissions; HuffPost separates personal essays from opinion; Chronicle of Higher Education asks for links to source material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the correct section (teacher submissions, blog, commentary) and follow its specialized requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a short headline or summary when requested
rubrics_metrics.description: Some outlets ask for a brief description or one-sentence theme that summarizes the piece (Buffalo News: 'theme that could be summarized in a single, complete sentence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a one-sentence theme or pitch summary where requested to clarify the piece’s focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting expectations for letters: single subject and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters often must 'deal with a single subject' and are encouraged to be concise ('Deal with a single subject', 'The shorter the better').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep letters tightly focused on one point and within stated short-word limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide headshot and short bio for credited op-eds
rubrics_metrics.description: Many outlets ask for a short bio and headshot to accompany the piece (examples: 'Include a short biographical paragraph', 'Include one- or two-sentence bio').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise bio (one or two sentences) and a web-ready headshot to include with the submission.
